name: acl_2025_accept_main_or_findings_given_commit

name: job_board_application_interview_rate
description: Derived from Brown, Setren & Topa Table 3: internet job-board applicants were 60.1% of 62,127 applicants and 40.0% of 1,811 interviewees, so ~1.94% of job-board applications led to an interview (all sources: 2.92%).
population: Applicants to a large, diverse US corporation (salaried positions; mean hire salary ~$103k), 2000s.

sources.citation: Brown, Setren & Topa (2016), 'Do Informal Referrals Lead to Better Matches? Evidence from a Firm's Employee Referral System', J. Labor Economics 34(1):161-209; NY Fed Staff Report 568 (Tables 3-4)

transferability_to_this_person: Single US firm, pre-LLM era, mostly experienced hires. Entry-level ML roles in India in 2026 likely have far more applicants per opening (AI-assisted mass applying), so cold-application interview rates are likely lower.
suggested_prior: Beta(1,40) for a cold online application to a selective ML role.

name: referred_application_interview_rate
description: Derived from Brown et al. Table 3: referred applicants were 6.1% of applicants but 21.4% of interviewees, so ~10.2% of referred applications led to an interview (~5x job-board). Regression: +7.3 pp interview probability (p<0.01). Fernandez & Galperin (2012, bank) report referrals ~5x as likely to be interviewed.

sources.citation: Brown, Setren & Topa (2016), 'Do Informal Referrals Lead to Better Matches? Evidence from a Firm's Employee Referral System', J. Labor Economics 34(1):161-209; NY Fed Staff Report 568 (Tables 3-4)
Fernandez & Weinberg (1997), 'Sifting and Sorting: Personal Contacts and Hiring in a Retail Bank', ASR 62(6):883-902

transferability_to_this_person: Ratio (~5x) is likely more transferable than the level. Selection: employees refer candidates they expect to succeed.
suggested_prior: Model as a multiplier on the cold rate: LogNormal(median 5x, 90% interval ~2-10x).

name: faculty_reply_rate_us_prospective_phd
description: Milkman, Akinola & Chugh field experiment: 67% of 6,548 US faculty (259 universities, 89 disciplines) replied to a fictional prospective PhD student asking to meet. White male names got more replies; Indian and Chinese names faced the most discrimination per the lead author. Low/high = reported subgroup range (e.g., 57% health sciences for women/minorities to 87% business for White men).
population: US tenure-track faculty, 2010 emails; sender = domestic prospective doctoral student requesting a short meeting.

sources.citation: Milkman, Akinola & Chugh (2015), 'What happens before? A field experiment exploring how pay and representation differentially shape bias on the pathway into organizations', J. Applied Psychology 100(6); overall rate via press coverage
NPR coverage of Milkman et al. (2014) quoting lead author on Indian/Chinese names

transferability_to_this_person: Upper bound for this person: the request was low-cost (a meeting) and from a prospective PhD applicant to the faculty's own program. An Indian undergraduate asking foreign faculty for a remote internship is a costlier ask, and Indian names were penalized. The overall 67% comes through press coverage, not the paper text.

population: Australian academics (senior lecturer+); sender = Australia-based prospective PhD student with fluent English.

sources.citation: Goldsmith, MacKenzie & Wynter (2024), 'Racial Bias in Academia: An Audit Experiment Revealing Disparities in Faculty Responses to Prospective Students', IJEPL 20(1)

name: weak_tie_job_transmission_per_tie
description: Rajkumar et al. (Science 2022): randomized PYMK experiments (20M+ LinkedIn members, 5 years, 2B new ties, 600k new jobs). Edge-level probability that a new tie transmits a job is of order 1e-3 (figure axis spans 0-0.004). Inverted-U in tie strength: moderately weak ties (~10 mutual connections per MIT Sloan coverage) and lowest-interaction ties produce the most mobility. Effects larger in digital/software industries.
unit: probability of job transmission per tie

sources.citation: Rajkumar, Saint-Jacques, Bojinov, Brynjolfsson & Aral (2022), 'A causal test of the strength of weak ties', Science 377(6612):1304-1310
MIT Sloan Ideas Made to Matter coverage (source of '10 mutual connections' peak)

transferability_to_this_person: Strong causal design for the shape; exact per-tie levels are only approximate (read from figure axes). Implies any single new weak tie has a tiny probability of producing a job; value comes from many ties.
suggested_prior: Per-tie job probability ~1e-3; do not model single contacts as likely job sources.

name: structural_holes_brokerage_effect
description: Burt (2004): among supply-chain managers at a large US electronics firm (673 per secondary summaries), brokers across structural holes had ideas judged more valuable and received higher compensation, better evaluations and more promotions.

sources.citation: Burt (2004), 'Structural Holes and Good Ideas', American Journal of Sociology 110(2):349-399

transferability_to_this_person: Correlational, single firm, corporate setting. Direction is credible; no transferable magnitude found.

name: ai_speedup_copilot_greenfield_task
description: Peng et al. (2023) RCT: developers with GitHub Copilot finished a JavaScript HTTP-server task 55.8% faster (95% CI 21-89%); mean 71 vs 161 min. Success rate +7 pp (not significant).
population: 95 Upwork freelance developers (45 treated / 50 control; analysis on completers), 2022, one small greenfield task.

sources.citation: Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon & Demirer (2023), 'The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot', arXiv:2302.06590

transferability_to_this_person: Best case for AI: small, well-specified greenfield task with a test suite. Little transfer to multi-week research projects.

name: ai_productivity_customer_support
description: Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond: AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% (working paper; 15% in QJE version) on average, ~34% for novice/low-skill agents, little for the most experienced.
population: ~5,172-5,179 customer-support agents at one firm, 2020-21 staggered rollout.

sources.citation: Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025), 'Generative AI at Work', QJE (NBER w31161 earlier version)

transferability_to_this_person: Different task domain. The heterogeneity pattern (gains concentrated among novices) is the transferable part.

name: ai_productivity_inside_frontier_consulting
description: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023): BCG consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with >40% higher quality on 18 tasks inside the AI frontier.
unit: fractional reduction in time per task

sources.citation: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023), 'Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier', HBS Working Paper 24-013 (SSRN 4573321)

transferability_to_this_person: Knowledge-work tasks chosen to suit GPT-4.

name: ai_correctness_penalty_outside_frontier
description: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023): on a task designed to be outside GPT-4's frontier, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct (control ~84.5%; AI groups ~60-70%).
unit: change in probability of a correct answer (pp)

sources.citation: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023), 'Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier', HBS Working Paper 24-013 (SSRN 4573321)

transferability_to_this_person: Directly relevant to research and evaluation work: AI help can lower correctness on tasks beyond model competence, and users do not notice. Supports adding a 'silent error' term for AI-assisted research.

name: ai_productivity_enterprise_field_experiments
description: Cui, Demirer et al.: pooled RCTs at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm found +26.08% completed tasks (SE 10.3%) with an AI code-completion assistant; larger gains for less experienced developers.
unit: fractional increase in completed tasks (low/high ~ +/-2 SE)

sources.citation: Cui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng & Salz, 'The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers', Management Science (DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535)

transferability_to_this_person: Completion-era tools, enterprise settings; output measured as task counts (PRs), not value.

name: ai_speedup_google_enterprise_rct
description: Paradis et al. (2024): Google's internal AI features cut time on a complex enterprise task by ~21% (raw 96 vs 114 min); the confidence interval is wide.

sources.citation: Paradis et al. (2024), 'How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial', arXiv:2410.12944 (ICSE-SEIP 2025)

transferability_to_this_person: Single lab task; one secondary summary says the result is not significant with proficiency controls.

name: ai_slowdown_experienced_oss_devs_2025
description: METR (2025) RCT: experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with early-2025 AI tools (Cursor + Claude 3.5/3.7; 95% CI +2% to +39%). Developers forecast a 24% speedup and afterwards believed they had been ~20% faster.
unit: fractional increase in completion time (positive = slower)
population: 16 experienced developers, 246 tasks in their own mature repos (avg 5 years' experience), Feb-Jun 2025.

sources.citation: Becker, Rush et al. (METR, 2025), 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity', arXiv:2507.09089

transferability_to_this_person: Mature, familiar codebases and high quality bars. The person often works on new or unfamiliar code, where the authors expect larger speedups, but the forecast-vs-actual gap is the main lesson: self-reported AI speedups are unreliable.

name: ai_speedup_experienced_devs_late_2025_update
description: METR 2026 update (Aug 2025-Feb 2026; 57 devs, 800+ tasks, newer agentic tools): returning developers -18% time (CI -38% to +9%); new developers -4% (CI -15% to +9%). METR calls the estimate a bad proxy because of selection effects (developers refused to work without AI and withheld AI-suited tasks).
unit: fractional change in completion time (negative = faster; low/high = 95% CI for new developers)

sources.citation: METR, 'Uplift update' blog post (2026-02-24)

transferability_to_this_person: Both intervals include zero. Selection biases the speedup downward, so the true effect may be larger. No clean RCT exists for agentic tools on solo research workflows.
suggested_prior: Speedup multiplier on coding subtasks: LogNormal centred near 1.0-1.2x with a wide 90% interval (0.8-2.0x); apply only to coding, not to research thinking or writing.

name: ai_agent_cli_output_lift_microsoft_2026
description: Murphy-Hill et al. (2026): Microsoft engineers adopting Claude Code / Copilot CLI merged ~24% more PRs than a counterfactual, sustained over 4 months.
population: Tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers, early 2026 rollout.

sources.citation: Murphy-Hill, Butler & Savelieva (2026), 'Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI', arXiv:2607.01418

transferability_to_this_person: Observational (adopters self-select); PR count is a throughput proxy, not research value.

name: ai_agent_code_quality_effect
description: Agarwal, He & Vasilescu (2026): adopting autonomous coding agents in OSS repos raised static-analysis warnings ~18% and cognitive complexity ~39%; velocity gains were front-loaded and mostly where agents were the first AI tool.
population: Open-source repos in the AIDev dataset; staggered difference-in-differences.

sources.citation: Agarwal, He & Vasilescu (2026), 'AI IDEs or Autonomous Agents? Measuring the Impact of Coding Agents on Software Development', arXiv:2601.13597

transferability_to_this_person: Supports a technical-debt or rework cost term when modelling agent-heavy solo projects.

name: weekly_hours_output_proportional_threshold
description: Pencavel: output rises in proportion to hours below ~49 h/week; above that it rises at a decreasing rate, peaking near ~63 h. Output at 70 h was barely above output at 56 h. A weekly rest day mattered.
unit: hours per week (knee where output stops tracking hours)

sources.citation: Pencavel (2015), 'The Productivity of Working Hours', Economic Journal 125(589):2052-2076; IZA DP 8129 (2014)

transferability_to_this_person: Manual, shift-based work a century ago. Direction (diminishing returns past ~50 h) is widely accepted; the exact knee for creative cognitive work is unknown and likely lower.
suggested_prior: Concave output curve: linear to ~45-50 h, flat beyond ~60 h; treat the knee as uncertain.

name: sleep_restriction_cognitive_deficit
description: Van Dongen et al. (2003): 14 days of 6 h or less time-in-bed produced cognitive deficits equivalent to up to 2 nights of total sleep deprivation. Lapses rose near-linearly with cumulative wakefulness beyond 15.84 h/day. Subjects were largely unaware of the deficits.
unit: hours of daily wakefulness before deficits accumulate
population: 48 healthy adults aged 21-38 in a lab (4, 6 or 8 h TIB x 14 days; 3 nights TSD).

sources.citation: Van Dongen, Maislin, Mullington & Dinges (2003), 'The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness', Sleep 26(2):117-126

transferability_to_this_person: Strong lab evidence on vigilance (PVT) and working memory; transfer to complex research work is plausible but not measured. 'Unaware of deficits' implies self-reports of fine-on-6h are unreliable.
suggested_prior: Model chronic <7 h sleep as a cumulative productivity and error-rate penalty that self-assessment does not detect.

name: task_switch_cost
description: Task-switching costs: responses are slower and more error-prone right after a switch (hundreds of ms per switch in lab tasks); costs grow with rule complexity and unfamiliarity, and preparation reduces but does not eliminate them (residual cost).
population: Lab participants on simple classification/arithmetic tasks.

sources.citation: Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans (2001), 'Executive control of cognitive processes in task switching', JEP:HPP 27(4):763-797
Monsell (2003), 'Task switching', Trends in Cognitive Sciences 7(3):134-140

transferability_to_this_person: Robust for millisecond lab switches; no credible measurement for switching between multi-day projects (e.g., paper vs ARC agent vs job applications). Popular figures like '40% productivity loss' or '23 minutes to refocus' are extrapolations, not these papers' results.
suggested_prior: Represent project switching as a scenario parameter (setup cost of 0.5-2 h per switch), explicitly labelled as assumption.

name: practice_curve_functional_form
description: Practice curves: Newell & Rosenbloom (1981) proposed a power law; Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000) refit 40 datasets (7,910 series, 475 subjects) and found the exponential fits individual data better, with the power law partly an artifact of averaging.

sources.citation: Newell & Rosenbloom (1981), 'Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice', in Anderson (ed.), Cognitive Skills and Their Acquisition
Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000), 'The power law repealed: The case for an exponential law of practice', Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 7(2):185-207

transferability_to_this_person: Contested. For one person, use exponential (or APEX) learning curves with a plateau; avoid power laws fitted to group averages.
suggested_prior: Per-skill exponential: time_n = asymptote + (initial - asymptote) * exp(-n/k).

name: spacing_optimal_gap_fraction_of_retention
description: Spacing: distributed practice beats massed practice (meta-analysis of 839 assessments, 317 experiments). Optimal gap between study sessions is ~20-40% of a 1-week retention interval, falling to ~5-10% for a 1-year interval.
unit: gap as fraction of retention interval
population: Verbal recall tasks; Cepeda 2008 had >1,350 online participants.

sources.citation: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006), 'Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis', Psychological Bulletin 132(3):354-380
Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler (2008), 'Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention', Psychological Science 19(11):1095-1102

transferability_to_this_person: Robust for fact recall; transfer to complex skills (e.g., interview prep, ML theory) is plausible but weaker.

name: planning_fallacy_duration_ratio_thesis
description: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994) Study 1: honors-thesis students predicted 33.9 days, took 55.5 days (actual/predicted = 1.64). Only 29.7% finished by their best guess and 48.7% by their worst-case guess (48.6 days).

sources.citation: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994), 'Exploring the planning fallacy', JPSP 67(3):366-381

transferability_to_this_person: Highly relevant: academic projects, same life stage. Small N. Even worst-case estimates were exceeded about half the time.
suggested_prior: Duration multiplier on self-estimates: LogNormal(median 1.6, sigma 0.4); P(on time) ~0.3.

name: planning_fallacy_on_time_rate
description: Buehler et al. (1994) Studies 2-3: students finished 37.1% of academic and 42.5% of nonacademic projects by their predicted time while reporting ~70-74% confidence (Study 3: 43.6%).

sources.citation: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994), 'Exploring the planning fallacy', JPSP 67(3):366-381

transferability_to_this_person: Overconfidence of ~30 pp between stated certainty and hit rate is the transferable quantity.
suggested_prior: Beta(4,6) for P(task done by own estimate).

name: it_project_cost_overrun_tail
description: Flyvbjerg & Budzier (2011): 1,471 IT projects, mean cost overrun 27%, but 1 in 6 was a 'black swan' averaging ~200% cost overrun. Follow-up (JMIS 2022, 5,392 projects) finds a power-law tail; a secondary summary reports tail alpha ~0.92 (unverified).
population: IT projects in public and private organizations, multiple countries.

sources.citation: Flyvbjerg & Budzier (2011), 'Why Your IT Project May Be Riskier Than You Think', HBR; arXiv:1304.0265
Flyvbjerg, Budzier et al. (2022), 'The Empirical Reality of IT Project Cost Overruns: Discovering A Power-Law Distribution', JMIS 39(3):607-639; arXiv:2210.01573

transferability_to_this_person: Organizational projects, not solo research. The transferable lesson is fat tails: use heavy-tailed (lognormal-plus-Pareto or power-law) overrun distributions, not normal ones.

name: software_task_estimate_error_factor
description: SiP dataset (8,252 tasks): 30% underestimated, 37% exact, 33% overestimated; geometric mean actual/estimate ~1.9 for underestimates and ~0.47 for overestimates (roughly a factor of 2 either way).
unit: actual / estimate ratio (geometric mean of underestimated tasks)
population: Tasks at one commercial software company (SiP), ~10 years.

sources.citation: Derek Jones, 'Over/under estimation factor for most estimates' (analysis of the public SiP task dataset)
Jorgensen et al., Simula report on measurement of software development effort overrun

transferability_to_this_person: Professional team estimates with time logging; analysis on a researcher's blog. Supports lognormal-style multiplicative errors; Jorgensen notes p50 planning leads to average overruns because of skew.

name: hf_zerogpu_pro_daily_quota
description: Hugging Face ZeroGPU daily quota for a PRO account: 40 min/day (free 5, unauthenticated 2, Enterprise 60), resets 24h after first use. Hardware is NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell: 'large' = half GPU, 48 GB (1x quota), 'xlarge' = full GPU, 96 GB (2x quota). Beyond quota: $1 per 10 GPU-minutes. Gradio SDK only; default 60 s per call; no torch.compile (AoT only); PRO can host 10 ZeroGPU Spaces.
population: Hugging Face PRO accounts, as of docs accessed 2026-10-09.

sources.citation: Hugging Face Hub docs, 'Spaces ZeroGPU'
gpuperhour.com, 'Free Cloud GPUs in 2026' (read Kaggle/Colab docs on 2026-09-21; secondary)

transferability_to_this_person: Correction to the profile assumption: ZeroGPU is no longer documented as H200; it is RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell. 40 min/day (20 min at xlarge) suits demos and short eval bursts, not training or 56k-translation batch runs.

name: kaggle_free_gpu_weekly_quota
description: Kaggle free GPU: ~30 h/week as commonly reported (shown in account settings; not stated in docs); sessions max 12 h for CPU/GPU, 9 h for TPU; TPU ~20 h/week. Hardware: T4 x2 or P100 class.

sources.citation: gpuperhour.com, 'Free Cloud GPUs in 2026' (read Kaggle/Colab docs on 2026-09-21; secondary)

transferability_to_this_person: Weekly quota floats; check account settings. Session caps are from Kaggle docs as quoted on 2026-09-21. Kaggle docs pages were JS-rendered and not machine-readable at access.

name: colab_free_session_limit
description: Google Colab free tier: sessions 'at most 12 hours, depending on availability and your usage patterns'; GPU access 'heavily restricted'; Colab does not publish usage limits and they fluctuate.

sources.citation: Google Colab FAQ (official)

transferability_to_this_person: Unreliable for planned experiments; model as stochastic availability.

name: india_msr_research_fellow_salary
description: MSR India Research Fellow pay: third-party listing estimates Rs 14-16.5 lakh per year (~Rs 1.2-1.4 lakh/month).
population: MSR India Research Fellows (1-2 year post-BTech/MTech appointments).

sources.citation: Prosple listing for Microsoft India Research Fellowship (third-party salary estimate)

transferability_to_this_person: Estimate from a job aggregator, not Microsoft. Treat as a range.

name: india_ai4bharat_residency_stipend
description: AI4Bharat (IIT Madras) AI Residency research track: Rs 50,000/month stipend (one-year; for recent CS graduates). IIT-M RBCDSAI post-baccalaureate fellowship: Rs 40,000-60,000/month (2021-22 postings).
population: Recent BTech graduates in IIT Madras AI programs.

sources.citation: IndiaAI news, 'IITM AI Residency Program - Research Track' (AI4Bharat; undated posting)

transferability_to_this_person: Postings are undated or old (2021-22); current amounts may differ.

name: india_sarvam_internship_stipend
description: Sarvam AI: summer internship up to Rs 50,000/month; AI Residency up to Rs 1 lakh/month (undated AIM report). The 2026 listing does not disclose a stipend.

sources.citation: Analytics India Magazine, 'Sarvam AI launches AI residency program offering up to INR 1 lakh monthly' (undated)

transferability_to_this_person: Undated trade-press report; 'up to' figures are ceilings.

name: india_google_intern_stipend
description: Google India SWE intern stipend: self-reported Glassdoor entries for Bengaluru 2025-26 cluster around Rs 1 lakh/month (range ~Rs 0.5-2 lakh). No official figure.

sources.citation: Glassdoor India, Google SDE Internship salaries (self-reported)

transferability_to_this_person: Self-reported, small sample, may mix roles. Student Researcher pay not found.

name: india_entry_ml_engineer_salary
description: Entry-level (0-1 y) ML/AI engineer pay in India: vendor guides cluster at Rs 6-8 LPA, with upper bands to Rs 12-14 LPA; AI research engineers at well-funded startups and labs reportedly Rs 15-30 LPA (weak sources).
population: Indian freshers in AI/ML engineering roles, 2026.

sources.citation: Instahyre, 'AI Engineer Salary in India' (May 2026; platform hiring data, method undisclosed)
Scaler, 'Machine Learning Engineer Salary in India 2026' (vendor guide)
Second Talent ML engineer India rate card (Sep 2026; vendor)

transferability_to_this_person: No credible median found (no official statistics; vendors have commercial interests). Tier-1 product and research labs pay well above this band; service companies below. Label as a range in any simulation.
suggested_prior: Bimodal scenario: mass-market Rs 6-10 LPA vs research/product lab Rs 15-30 LPA; do not average.
